claims.statement: A sample mean varies from sample to sample, and the way that variation occurs is described by the sampling distribution of the mean; the standard deviation of that sampling distribution is called the standard error of the estimate of the mean.
claims.scope: A mean estimated from a sample drawn from a population, in the setting the source addresses, which is reporting and interpreting medical research. The source presents the sampling distribution as the description of how the sample mean varies and the standard error as its spread.
claims.uncertainty: The source states the relationship without conditions on the population's shape; the conditions under which the sampling distribution can be treated as normal are handled separately in this lesson through the central limit theorem.

claims.statement: The standard error of a sample mean equals the standard deviation divided by the square root of the sample size, so the standard error falls as the sample size increases, while the standard deviation does not tend to change as the sample grows; this relation is what underlies a sample size calculation.
claims.scope: The mean of a sample of independent observations. The source states the relation in the form SE = SD divided by the square root of the sample size and names its use in planning the size of a controlled trial.
claims.uncertainty: The relation assumes the observations entering the mean are independent. Repeated measurements on the same people, cluster designs, and other structured samples have fewer effective independent observations than rows, so dividing by the square root of the row count would overstate the precision; the lesson flags this and does not teach the corrected methods.

claims.statement: The standard error of the mean is a measure of the precision of the sample mean and is the quantity quoted to indicate the uncertainty around an estimated mean, whereas the standard deviation is the quantity quoted to say how widely scattered the individual measurements are.
claims.scope: Reporting a mean and a measure of dispersion beside it in a research paper or an audit report. The source gives this as the rule for choosing between the two quantities.
claims.uncertainty: Precision here means how repeatable the estimate is under resampling. It says nothing about whether the estimate is aimed at the right population, which is a question about how the sample was reached and which no standard error addresses.

claims.statement: For data with a normal distribution about 95% of individuals have values within two standard deviations of the mean, and about 95% of observations of any distribution usually fall within those two-standard-deviation limits, though the observations outside them may all lie at one end.
claims.scope: Individual observations in a sample or population, used in this lesson only to give the standard deviation a concrete reading so it can be set beside the standard error. The normal case is exact; the source's broader statement about any distribution is offered as a usual pattern.
claims.uncertainty: The source qualifies the general version with 'usually' and warns that the observations outside the limits may all be at one end, which matters for the skewed cohort in this block.

claims.statement: A plus-or-minus sign joining a second figure to a reported mean does not itself indicate whether that figure is a standard deviation or a standard error; a review of 88 articles published in 2002 found that 12 of them, 14%, failed to identify which measure of dispersion was reported, and the BMJ's policy is to remove plus-or-minus signs and ask authors to state clearly which quantity is quoted.
claims.scope: Reporting practice in medical journals. The 88-article figure is a finding the source cites from a review of published articles from 2002; the editorial policy is the BMJ's own, described as shared by many other journals.
claims.uncertainty: The 14% figure describes one review of one year's articles in a particular field and is not an estimate of current practice across the literature. The lesson uses it as evidence that the ambiguity is real and common enough to have prompted editorial action, and not as a current prevalence.

claims.statement: The sampling-distribution principle applies to quantities other than a mean, including a proportion, a regression coefficient, and contrasts between two samples such as a risk ratio or a difference between two means; every such estimate carries uncertainty from sampling variation and has a standard error that indicates the degree of that uncertainty.
claims.scope: Statistics estimated from a sample. The source states the extension of the principle and the existence of a standard error for each such estimate; it does not give the formula for any of them, and this lesson does not supply one either.
claims.uncertainty: How a standard error is calculated differs from statistic to statistic, and some require methods this lesson does not cover. The lesson transfers the reasoning and marks the arithmetic as belonging to later lessons.

claims.statement: The central limit theorem holds that as the sample size becomes large, the sampling distribution of the mean becomes approximately normal regardless of the distribution of the original variable, is centred at the population mean of that variable, and has a standard deviation approaching the population standard deviation divided by the square root of the sample size.
claims.scope: The mean of a random sample of independent observations from a population with a finite variance. Both sources state the result in these terms, one as the theoretical justification for the wide applicability of the normal distribution and the other as a review written for a clinical readership.
claims.uncertainty: The result is asymptotic: it describes what happens as the sample size grows, and it does not certify any particular finite sample. How large a sample must be before the approximation is usable depends on how far the population departs from normality, which the lesson treats as a judgement rather than a threshold.

claims.statement: A skewed population distribution does not prevent the distribution of sample means from approaching normality as the sample size increases, and the sample means gather more closely around the population mean as that size grows; a sample size of about 30 is the conventional point at which the Student's t distribution is treated as equalling the normal distribution.
claims.scope: Random samples drawn from a population, as demonstrated in the source through the complete set of samples from a small skewed population. The size-30 figure is reported there as an established convention in statistical practice.
claims.uncertainty: The figure of 30 is a working convention and not a property of the theorem. Strongly skewed or heavy-tailed populations, and samples in which one observation can move the mean substantially, need considerably more than 30 before the approximation is safe. The lesson states this limit explicitly and gives a case where the convention fails.

claims.statement: The US National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases states that a fasting plasma glucose result of 99 mg/dL or below is normal, 100 to 125 mg/dL indicates prediabetes, and 126 mg/dL or above indicates diabetes, that a doctor will usually use a second test to confirm a diabetes diagnosis, and that fasting means having nothing to eat or drink except sips of water.
claims.scope: Reference values for the fasting plasma glucose test as published for a general US audience at the access date. Quoted in this lesson only so that the audit-planning case has a real interval width against which to judge whether an estimate is precise enough for its purpose.
claims.uncertainty: Thresholds and their qualifications are set by clinical bodies, can be revised, and differ in presentation between countries and guidelines. The lesson makes no diagnostic, monitoring, or treatment recommendation and its clinic and cohort are invented.
